pages.transcription:
Newyork, 25.4.1941.

Dear Hanna and Manfred,
I believe that for some time now I have not
written you more than just a few lines or a page in a hurry, and to-day
it is again the same - I don't know whether it is the asthma-business
which makes me more lazy or the doctors with their injections and tests
who take all my time, in any case I don't seem to get round to do all I
want to do, and also the work has been somewhat neglected these last
weeks. Now at last the tests are finished and I expect that I can get
one of the doctors to give you a short medical report. As far as I under-
stand, they consider me a perfect allergic case, sensitive according to
the tests especially to dust and some of my own nose- and throat bacte-
rias. They'll start making injections with those things and say that in
most cases they have good results in immunising. Unfortunately for us
the result will not show up definitely before a few week's treatment,and
Stefan especially is anxious for a quick result. I have learned more
patience and am already satisfied that the calcium injections (although
only as long as they are continued) definitively help. It is of course
disappointing that this whole business which I believed to have got over
many years ago, has suddenly come back. But it is in no way as bad as it
was then, the treatment is more effective, and now I am hoping for the
new treatment. So don't believe completely Stefan's a little exaggerated
reports and remember that he has never known me with asthma and so feels
terribly disappointed that a few injections did not completely heal it.
Now that is enough of my health and I hope I shall not have to mention
it again. But as he started telling you about it, I wanted to make the
real situation as clear as possible.
About Eva. We sent you a number of photos - in our
opinion excellent ones - by registered air-mail last week (to Bath) and
hope that you already got them. I think they tell you more about her than
many descriptions, and you see from them that she has ~~xxxxx~~ grown taller
and slightly thinner, that she looks strong and healthy, and in excellent
spirits. Of course there are moments where - like all of us - she is
longing to be home and again with you - but we would be very disappointed
if she did not feel that way sometimes, and they really are only moments,
and she is absolutely happy and at home at Amity Hall. Marion Ullstein,
a thirteen year old girl - I am sure she wrote you about her - is her
best friend there, and these two, together with two other boys of about
12 or 13,feel themselves as the "big children" against the small ones,
which seems to be quite a nice feeling. I have met Marion when I was
in Croton and I liked her very much, also one of the "big boys", Rudi.
The other boy I have not yet seen. In the summer vacations some of the
smaller children will go away and apparently some bigger children will
come, Marion will also stay in Croton. I could have arranged to send Eva
to a camp for the summer, but it is hot everywhere, unless you go very
far away, and Eva herself said she liked it so much at Amity Hall, she
would not like to go away. And Mrs. Sch. will run the house in the va-
cations just like one of the camps, that is to say entertain and keep
the children busy with all sorts of occupations, games, excursions and
sports. When I have seen her again I shall be able to tell you more in
detail, Eva only told me a little of what she planned to do with them,
and also spoke of learning French and reading German. If Mrs. Sch.
wrote you about Eva's starting Latin, I suppose this too is in her plan,
and as she has x the doctor's degree in philology (Eva proudly told me
that she even knows Greek) this speaks for her ability and knowledge.
By the way, Evas friend Marion has been in school in Switzerland and
speaks English, French and German equally well. And Eva says that she
often talks to her in French at night and that she is beginning to under-
stand. The school system, as regards the teaching of languages, is

2

quite different. Eva is now in the 8th grade, and until she gets into
the 9th grade (next February) she won't have neither French nor Latin.
The progressive school where I first intended to send her, does teach
French earlier, but nevertheless I am very glad she does not go there.
From all I hear - and I take every opportunity to speak with parents
about this - it is much better for her education to go to a real school
even though the other school had a very good reputation. The whole
school system is very different here from the English one, but altogether
I understand that in the Public School they have the best chances of
learning, and the one she goes to is supposed to be good. And in Mrs.
Sch.'s house they are sure to have more stimulation than in an American
home. - Sunday I have been with Eva to see Harriet's sister Elizabeth.
She lives in Yonkers, halfway between Newyork and Croton, and Eva was
brought to the station, travelled that half hour alone and was met at
the station again by me. Elizabeth has two children, a girl, Nancy, of
about 11, and a boy, Philipp, of 13, and as far as I can judge, Eva
liked the girl and vice versa, and they seemed both delighted at Eli-
zabeth's suggestion that Eva should soon spend a weekend with them.
I like the idea very much, Yonkers is very conveniently situated, except
the way to and from the station Eva can travel alone, Elizabeth and her
husband are really very nice, and I liked the children very much, too.
They are both lively and intelligent, as good-looking as Harriet's
children but much more natural and agreeable to my taste- and I suppose
to Eva's taste too. I think you too will like the idea to know pleasant
relatives near Eva in addition to us. As to Salmon's they are typically
American as all our other American friends in so far as you cannot get
any relationship with them except when you actually have something de-
finite to say or a definite appointment to make. Eva has been there for
a weekend and apparently they wanted to invite her for the Easter holi-
days. But when Eva said that she was going to spend those with us,
nothing more was heard of them in spite of several letters and an Easter
card and the pyjamas which Eva sent them. If I can judge from my ex-
perience with other Americans, especially Rose and Huebsch, Salmon's
will one day again ring up Eva and invite her - but there is not such a
thing as keeping up a relationship by just writing or phonecalle. -
While Eva was here, we had lunch with Franz Neumann, and he too promised
to drive out to visit her one day. I have the same idea as you that -
whether we remain here or not - Eva should have as many contact with
friends besides us as possible, it will make it more pleasant for her,
the more people she has to go to and who visit her. My sister-in-law,
whom from now on I shall call with her first name Stefanie is genuinely
eager to look after Eva too, to invite her, to go out with her and to
spoil her, and I believe, she even thought me rather cruel and careless
that I did not take Eva to a show every day. But I assure you that even
though Eva had to spend more time than I would have liked, accompanying
me to the doctor etc. she liked being with us immensely and we liked
having her with us just as much. But then she liked also going back
to the children and her normal routine, and this is just as it should be.
I must say I envied her, going back to the country. - I am glad that
you sent me Miss Baker's address. I'll ask Eva to write her soon and
perhaps add a few words myself. I am sure Miss Baker sometimes comes to
Newyork and it would be nice for both of them to meet again.
Now, inspite of my excuse at the beginning, I have written you
a long letter and hope you will retaliate with an even longer one.
Thanks for all your repeated birthday wishes. Fortunately letters take
hardly a fortnight lately, and I was happy to receive your letter of
the 11th April already yesterday, the 24th. I hope our letters reach you
just as quickly.
Love and kisses, and
kindest regards to the Rosemount and Regency Lodge inhabitants. Lotte.
